text: Why do billionaires always start their own charitable foundations?
It's not just about helping others.
Imagine Rich Rick just made ten million dollars.
The IRS wants about three point seven million. Rick says no.
So he starts a private foundation: the Rich Rick Foundation.
He donates the ten million. It's charity, so it's tax-deductible.
Thirty percent of his income counts this year, the rest over five years. His tax bill drops by over a million.
But Rick didn't give it away. He named himself president.
The foundation can pay him a salary. Legal, if it's reasonable.
His family sits on the board. Also legal.
The private jet? Only for foundation trips. Vacations would be self-dealing.
The foundation only has to give away five percent a year. The rest stays invested, under his control.
Those investments can keep growing for decades.
And when he dies, it skips the forty percent estate tax.
His kids can take over the foundation, and keep drawing salaries.
And the best part? Everyone calls him a philanthropist.
Want more tricks the rich use? Follow for part two.
